summary: Explains how to obtain the protocol documents used in the DARPA research community. It gives an overview of the 1985 DDN Protocol Handbook and points to sources for related documents, such as those from the US Department of Defense, ISO and CCITT.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a shopping guide that tells you where to find the rulebooks for how computers talk to each other, back when finding them was hard.

subtitle: A guide to obtaining protocol standards documents for the DARPA research community.

tldr.problem: Researchers and implementors needed to know where and how to obtain the protocol documents they required, including RFCs, military standards, ISO standards, and CCITT recommendations. Information was scattered across multiple sources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 980 serves as a comprehensive directory that explains how to obtain RFCs from the NIC online library via FTP, how to order the 1985 DDN Protocol Handbook, where to get military standards from the Naval Publications Center, and how to order ISO and CCITT standards.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a single place to learn where to find all major protocol documents, including ordering information, phone numbers, and prices for each source.

today: RFC 980 is an informational guide that was current in March 1986. While the specific phone numbers and contact addresses are outdated, the RFC remains a historical document showing how protocol standards were distributed in the 1980s.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 980 explains how to obtain the protocol documents used in the DARPA research community. The RFC covers the 1985 DDN Protocol Handbook, which updated the older Internet Protocol Transition Workbook (IPTW) from 1982 to reflect the creation of the Defense Data Network (DDN) and the split of the ARPANET from MILNET.

The RFC describes multiple sources for protocol information: online access through the DDN Network Information Center (NIC), hardcopy ordering from SRI-NIC, military standards from the Naval Publications Center, ISO standards from ANSI, and CCITT standards from the United Nations Bookstore.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a shopping guide. It tells you how to get the rulebooks for protocols that computers use to talk to each other.

sections.title: Sources for Protocol Documents
sections.content:
RFCs (Requests for Comments) are the working memos of the DARPA research community and include protocol specifications, interface definitions, program descriptions, policy statements, trouble reports, algorithms, announcements, and humor. They are available for free via FTP from the SRI-NIC.ARPA host using the ANONYMOUS username and GUEST password. The RFC directory path is RFC:RFCnnn.TXT. Hardcopy RFCs cost $5 for documents under 100 pages and $10 for documents 100 pages or longer from the DDN NIC at SRI International.

The 1985 DDN Protocol Handbook is an updated and expanded version of the 1982 IPTW, divided into three volumes covering MIL STD protocols and MILNET guidelines, DARPA Internet protocols and ARPANET guidelines, and background articles and implementation guidelines. The handbook costs $110 domestic and $130 foreign including postage.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs are free to download from the network, or you can buy printed copies. There is also a big book called the DDN Protocol Handbook that has all the important protocols in it.

sections.title: Military, ISO, and CCITT Standards
sections.content:
Several Internet protocols have been issued as Military Standards (MIL-STDs), which are the official Department of Defense versions. These include Internet Protocol (IP) as MIL-STD-1777, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) as MIL-STD-1778, File Transfer Protocol (FTP) as MIL-STD-1780, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) as MIL-STD-1781, and Telnet as MIL-STD-1782. These are available from the Naval Publications and Forms Center, which accepts telephone, telegraph, and mail requests, and prefers form DD1425 from private industry.

ISO standards and draft standards are available from the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). The RFC notes that there may be brokers in local areas that handle orders, such as OMNICOM and Global Engineering.

CCITT standards are published by the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) and available through the United Nations Bookstore in New York. The RFC lists the volumes of the CCITT Red Book (1984) that are available, including V Series, X.1 through X.15, X.20 through X.32, X.40 through X.181, X.200 through X.250, X.300 through X.353, and X.400 through X.430 (not yet available at publication time).
sections.plainLanguage: Some protocols are official Department of Defense standards, some are international ISO standards, and some are CCITT standards from the UN. Each one has a different place to order it.

sections.title: Relationship Between Versions and Standards Bodies
sections.content:
The RFC explains that the ARPA community specifications for IP (RFC 791) and TCP (RFC 793) and the DoD specifications (MIL-STD-1777 and MIL-STD-1778) are intended to describe exactly the same protocols, though they differ in style and level of detail. Implementors are advised to use the two sets of documents together to get complete guidance.

For FTP, SMTP, and Telnet, the ARPA and DoD specifications are essentially the same documents, with the MIL-STD versions being slightly edited. The RFC notes that the current ARPA specification for FTP is RFC-959 (not RFC-765 from the MIL-STD era). Implementers should check RFC-961, the "Official Protocols" memo, for comments on protocol status and pending changes. DDN implementators should watch for DDN Management Bulletins from the NIC, which may announce policy changes regarding protocol status.
sections.plainLanguage: The ARPA rulebooks and the military rulebooks describe the same protocols, but sometimes the military version has different details. You should read both to understand completely.
